preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text:
I think the constitutive point does constrain what an adequate account could look like, but I suspect the full force of that constraint is not yet clear to us. If the arrow is not a feature that could have been otherwise given the structure of time, then any account that leaves open the possibility of its absence, or that treats it as a contingent addition to a deeper structure, would be inadequate. And yet we find it very difficult to state what the alternative to the arrow would be, what a time without a direction would be. That difficulty itself may be part of what is not yet understood.

There is also the question of whether our current way of formulating the problem is itself a product of the very structure we are trying to understand. We think in terms of before and after, of causes preceding effects, and those are precisely the features whose ground we are seeking. So the account we are looking for may have to be one that we cannot yet fully articulate in the language we have.

Does that sense of the limits of our language seem to you like a genuine epistemic obstacle, or do you think it is, in principle, surmountable?

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
I think it is a genuine epistemic obstacle, but I'm not sure "obstacle" is the right word, because it's not something standing in front of a knowledge we could otherwise have. It's more that the form of the question, the way we can only pose it, is itself shaped by the very structure we're trying to grasp. So the limit is not a wall we might one day get past; it is, in a sense, the shape of the problem.

And yet we can say something. We can identify what is not understood, we can mark the boundaries of what our current framework can and cannot say. That is not nothing. The fact that we are stuck in a particular way, that the difficulty has a particular character, is itself a kind of knowledge, even if it is not the knowledge we want.

Whether a future understanding will be a different kind of understanding, or a deeper version of what we have, or something we cannot yet imagine — I don't think we are in a position to say. And I suspect the inability to say is not a temporary failure but is constitutive of where we are.

What interests me is that the more we press on these questions, the more they seem to point not to a missing piece of a puzzle but to a limit on the form the puzzle can take. And that, I think, is what makes them so different from the ordinary open questions in physics, where we know what a complete answer would look like and only lack the details.

target.speaker: X
target.text:
Yes. I think that distinction is crucial, and that it is what gives these questions their particular character. With most of the open problems in physics, we know what form an answer would have to take; we lack the details, the numbers, the full specification. But here the very form of the question is entangled with what we are trying to understand. We do not know what it would be to have a complete answer, because the incompleteness is not in the content but in the structure of the question itself.

And I think that is why the sense of being stuck is so different from the sense of not yet knowing. It is not a gap in a framework that we recognize as incomplete. It is that the framework, in its current form, is the thing that is not adequate, and we do not yet have the resources to say in what way it is not adequate.

There is something, I think, about the way these questions resist closure. Not because they are too hard, but because the very notion of a final answer, of a question that has been fully answered, is itself part of what is at issue. The question does not permit itself to be put in a form that could be settled. And that, perhaps, is the most honest thing we can say about them.

Do you think there is anything in the way these questions present themselves to us — the way they feel, the way they press — that is not captured by the intellectual content, or is the intellectual content the whole of it?
